title: The Haskalah
hookLine: the Jewish Enlightenment, joining Jewish and general learning

lines: TELESCOPE, IN THE LANGUAGE OF THE PSALMS?
AN ANCIENT LANGUAGE, A NEW WORLD.
cards: How do you say telescope in the language of the Psalms? Or vaccine, or electricity, or newspaper? The Bible never needed those words.
Hebrew had long been a language of prayer, study and law, while people spoke something else at home.
Then a group of Jewish writers decided Hebrew should be able to talk about everything: planets and poetry, chemistry and history.
They printed journals in Hebrew about science, and wrote Hebrew poems that had nothing to do with the synagogue. They were stretching an ancient language to fit a new world.

teach.b: The movement is called the Haskalah, the Jewish Enlightenment, and its followers were maskilim. It began among Jews in Germany in Mendelssohn's circle, and later moved east, into the towns and cities of the Pale.
Jews, they said, should learn the languages of the countries they lived in, and mathematics, science, history and useful trades, alongside the Torah, not instead of it.
They wanted Jewish schools that taught both, and Hebrew itself reborn as a living language of literature.
They liked to point back to scholars like Maimonides, who studied philosophy and medicine and wrote some of the great works of Jewish law. An old line in the Mishnah fits their hopes.
In Pirkei Avot, Ben Zoma asks: who is wise?

teach.h: WHO IS WISE? WHO LEARNS FROM EVERYONE.
teach.b: The one who learns from every person. Wisdom, on that reading, can come from anywhere, and a learned Jew can take it in without losing who they are. That was the maskilim's bet.

teach.h: A FIERCE ARGUMENT, AND HEBREW STRETCHING.
teach.b: Not everyone accepted it, and the argument was fierce. Traditional rabbis, Hasidic and non-Hasidic alike, warned that the Haskalah was a road out of Judaism, and could point to young people who walked it all the way out.
Some maskilim, in turn, mocked the traditional world, sometimes cruelly. Each camp had its own picture of Jewish life in a new age.
Meanwhile the Hebrew journals kept printing, stretching the language of the Psalms to name things it had never named before.

how: The Haskalah's legacy lives on in modern Hebrew literature and in Jewish schools that teach both Jewish and general subjects, while some traditional communities still keep secular learning at a distance.

games.q: you're a maskil. what language do you choose for your new journal about science?
o: Hebrew, stretched to talk about everything.
only German, leaving Hebrew for prayer.
no journal; science isn't for Jews.
games.why: Haskalah writers printed journals and poems in Hebrew, stretching the ancient language to fit a new world.

practice: Bring to mind something from the ordinary world you know a little about: how plants grow, how money works, a piece of music, a law of physics.
Turn it slowly, the way a maskil might, and ask what a Torah teacher would find worth noticing in it, a pattern, a kind of order, a question about how to live; you don't need an answer.
